title: AI Helped With Homework. Did It Help on the Exam?

paper.title: Supporting or Replacing Students' Reasoning? Cognitive Offloading in AI-Assisted Proof Learning
paper.authors: Eason Chen, Sophia Judicke, Kayla Beigh, Xinyi Tang et al.
paper.affil: Carnegie Mellon University · The University of Hong Kong

stats.label: Exam points linked via chatbot use

rows: Chatbot: ask anything, no attempt needed
Feedback tool: submit your proof first
More chatbot use: lower exam scores
Feedback tool use: no negative link

takeaway.text: A better grade with A.I. isn't the same as what you can do alone.

lines: Good evening, everybody! Welcome to Behavior Decoded Tonight. I'm Kai.
Thank you, thank you. Look at you all, clapping like you finished your homework.
Speaking of homework. Tonight's question. If an A.I. helps you get a better grade on your homework, does that mean you actually learned the stuff?
Because I got a lot of good grades on homework in my life, and I still have no idea what a cosine is.
Here to explain it, our resident data scientist, the only person I know who double checks the appendix. Anne!
Hi! Thank you. And Kai, the cosine is still out there. It's waiting for you.
So tonight's paper was just posted on archive, by a team from Carnegie Mellon and the University of Hong Kong.

lines.sub: So tonight's paper was just posted on arXiv, by a team from Carnegie Mellon and the University of Hong Kong.

lines: And what did they look at?
A real university math course. Proof writing. Logic, sets, relations.
Relations! Finally, a math class that helps with my love life.
They studied one hundred fifty-three students who agreed to take part. And those students got an A.I. support system with two tools.

lines.sub: They studied 153 students who agreed to take part. And those students got an A.I. support system with two tools.

lines: Tool one is a chatbot. You can ask it any math question. It was instructed not to give final answers, only hints and questions back.
Like a wise old teacher on a mountain.
Tool two gives homework feedback. But here's the catch. You have to paste in your own proof attempt first. Then it critiques it.
So one says, ask me anything. The other says, show me what you've got.
Exactly. And everything was logged. Every message, every feedback request. Plus interviews with nineteen students.

lines.sub: Exactly. And everything was logged. Every message, every feedback request. Plus interviews with 19 students.

lines: So how do you test whether it helps? Just give it to everybody and see?
That's the clever part. After the first midterm, every student was randomly assigned. Basically a coin flip.
Seventy-five students got the A.I. tools right away. Seventy-eight had to wait until after the second midterm.

lines.sub: 75 students got the A.I. tools right away. 78 had to wait until after the second midterm.

lines: Team Wait. So for a few weeks you have two groups that are the same on average, except one has A.I. help. It's a randomized experiment with staggered access. Everyone gets the tool, just not at the same time.
Like when your friend gets the new phone first and you just have to watch.
Pretty much. And on the exams, no A.I. allowed. Just you and your brain.
Okay, so what happened? Did Team A.I. crush it?
On homework, yes. During those weeks, the early group scored about two and a half points higher, even after accounting for how they did on earlier homework.

lines.sub: On homework, yes. During those weeks, the early group scored 2.56 points higher, even after accounting for how they did on earlier homework.

lines: Then came the second midterm. No A.I. And the two groups were basically tied. The early group was even a little lower, but that gap was not statistically significant.
Wait. The homework got better, but the test didn't?
No detectable gain on the exam. And the exam is what you can do on your own.
So what does that mean for me?
It means a better homework score with A.I. doesn't automatically mean you'll do better without it. You have to check both.
Now part two. After the second midterm, everybody got access. And students could choose how much to use it.
So they counted messages to the chatbot and compared that to the third midterm. Every extra hundred messages was linked to about three points lower on that exam.

lines.sub: So they counted messages to the chatbot and compared that to the third midterm. Every extra 100 messages was linked to about 3 points lower on that exam.

lines: A hundred messages? Who sends a hundred messages to a chatbot?
You send a hundred messages to your group chat before lunch.
And that's after accounting for each student's earlier midterm score and their confidence. It also held up in a couple of extra checks.
So the chatbot made them worse at math!
Careful. This part is not a coin flip. Students chose how much to chat. So it's a correlation, not proof the chatbot caused it.
Okay. Then who were the heavy chatters?
At the start, students rated their confidence on a scale of one to seven. Statements like, I expect to do very well in this class.
I'd give myself a four. A very confident four.
Researchers call it self-efficacy. For each point higher, students sent about thirty-nine percent fewer chatbot messages, even comparing students with the same midterm score.

lines.sub: Researchers call it self-efficacy. For each point higher, students sent about 39% fewer chatbot messages, even comparing students with the same midterm score.

lines: So the less confident students leaned on it more.
Yes. Then a mediation analysis asks: does confidence connect to exam scores through chatbot use? It does, modestly. About point six two exam points per confidence point, through that route.

lines.sub: Yes. Then a mediation analysis asks: does confidence connect to exam scores through chatbot use? It does, modestly. About 0.62 exam points per confidence point, through that route.

lines: So lower confidence, more chatting, lower scores.
That's the pattern. The authors' interpretation is cognitive offloading. Handing the thinking over to the tool.
Think of a gym. If a robot lifts the weights for you, your workout log looks fantastic. Your arms don't change.
In one example in the paper, a student types, I don't know, tell me. Then, tell me the answer. And the chatbot hands over more and more of the steps.
That's me with my GPS. I don't know, just tell me where to turn.
What about the other tool? The show me your attempt one?
That's the contrast. Using the feedback tool, where you had to try first, was not linked to lower exam scores.
So the try first tool wins!
We can't say that. The study wasn't built to compare the two tools head to head. It just didn't show the same warning sign.
But the authors do recommend against using an open-ended chatbot as a tutor, and suggest exploring tools that ask students to attempt first.
Okay, fine print time. What can't this study tell us?
It's one course at one university, with students who volunteered. Other subjects, newer models, or different prompts might look different.
And the usage results are correlations. Maybe students who were already struggling simply asked for more help. The authors flag that themselves.
So the chatting might be a symptom, not the cause.
Could be. Offloading is an interpretation. They didn't measure how hard students were thinking, or whether they used other A.I. tools outside the system.
Possibly. And the final exam isn't in the study. Data collection stopped at the third midterm because of budget.
Even science runs out of snack money.
So the lesson is not, A.I. bad.
No. The lesson is, a better grade with A.I. isn't the same as what you can do alone.
So what do I actually do?
Try the problem yourself first. Then ask for feedback on your attempt. And if A.I. gives you a step, explain it back in your own words.
Explain it back. Got it. I'll start with the cosine.
That's our show! Anne, thank you. The paper is on archive, link in the description. I'm Kai, this has been Behavior Decoded Tonight. Good night, everybody!
